items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Fats Navarro, Freddy Webster, Red Allen, Rex Stuart, there was just so many great guys you could learn from.

ctx.x: You got that right. You make the notes count as you get older. Like Dizzy used to say, his chops ain’t what they used to be, and he doesn’t get ahold of that horn like he used to. I said, “Well, I told you a long time, Birks, you know, as you get older, you’re going to have to slow down.” And you know it does, you slow down. I never have wanted to play fast, dazzle as you say, with your ability to get over your horn, because guys wasn’t doing it when I was coming up. Louis Armstrong, he wasn’t dazzling anybody…

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: And Fats Navarro, what a talent he was, you know.

ctx.x: That was such a pity. That's so -- such great talents that have been -- careers have been shortened by that drug. And I think it's absolutely -- you know, it's -- I think people weak go for that. You know, they just want to follow somebody. They're not leaders, they're followers, you know. And they can be like Paul. Paul could be led into doing anything if he liked you. You could tell him -- you know, he was very weak, as far as that is concerned. Charlie Parker and those other guys were very strong because they…
And Fats Navarro, what a talent he was, you know. And when he first came to New York, he weighed 250 pounds. And I saw him just before he passed, he was weighing about 120 pounds.
Well, what was that? That wasn't just heroin, was it?
